Emerald City Leadership Network – Members' Survey
February 2024
Theme: Gillikin Growers Circle

Responses compiled by Rowan Bell, Community Manager.
Question 1: What’s a recent piece of work you’ve done or are planning, connected to your land or community?

I’m planning to propose a change at our next allotment committee meeting. We have a communal tool shed, and the key for the padlock goes missing more often than not. I’m going to suggest we fit a combination lock instead. Nothing grand, but it would save a lot of frustration and wasted time looking for that key.

This past autumn, I coordinated with three neighboring farms to plant a mixed hedge along a shared boundary line. It’s hawthorn, dogwood, and some early-flowering willow. The primary purpose is a windbreak for all our fields, but it will also provide crucial early pollen for my hives come spring. The scent of that willow bloom on a mild morning is something to look forward to.

Last month, I spent a morning calibrating our bagging scale specifically for bulk oatmeal orders. The Gillikin Breakfast Co-op supplies several programs across the country, and their orders come in very specific weights. The standard calibration was just a bit off for that volume and consistency. It’s accurate now, so they get exactly what they pay for, and we don’t give short measure.

The Branch Mill down in South Orchard had a slightly warped granite stone. Nothing dangerous, but it was affecting the grind. They don’t have the rig for resurfacing, so I brought over our hand-cranked grinding setup. Spent two afternoons working it back to flat. It’s quiet work. You listen to the stone.
Question 2: What’s a challenge you’re noticing in your area that others in the network might have insight on?

Water access. Our communal taps are on a timed system, which is fair, but the pressure drops terribly if more than two plots are watering at once. I’m wondering if any of the irrigation circles in Winkie or Quadling have dealt with low-pressure communal systems.

Unseasonable frosts after early budbreak. It’s a worry for the orchardists I work with, and for my own forage sources. I’ve heard some Winkie growers use wind machines, but that’s a big investment. Are there smaller-scale, cooperative methods being tried elsewhere?

Getting consistent, affordable feed grain delivered up here to the Falls. The transport costs are high, and the quality varies wildly from load to load. If other mills or livestock operations have found reliable suppliers or arranged group shipments, I’d like to hear about it.

Finding young people interested in learning the millwright trade. It’s steady work, but it’s not fast work. Most of us running these smaller mills are getting on in years. If a mill goes down, it can disrupt a whole community’s food. How are other trades guilds attracting apprentices?
Question 3: What’s one thing you’ve learned from another member of the Growers Circle, or from the network in general?

From Otis, actually. The idea that a hedge isn’t just a boundary, it’s a habitat and a resource. It made me look at the bramble patch at the back of the allotments differently. We’re leaving it be now for the birds and the bees.

Honor’s point about calibration. It seems obvious, but weighing feed for hives is different from weighing seed for planting. Accuracy matters in different ways. I’ve started checking my own scales against a known weight at the start of each season.

Merritt’s approach to repairs. The patience of it. When something here needs fixing, my first thought is often to call someone. His story about the millstone reminded me that we still have the knowledge and the tools for a lot of this work, if we take the time.

Celia’s endless patience with lists and logistics. I run a mill, not a committee, but watching how she manages the allotment waiting list and proposals has given me ideas for how to handle customer orders and repair schedules more clearly. It’s all just organized thinking.
